page.title: OSHA 1910.145 Sign Requirements: Danger, Caution and Safety Instruction Signs
page.body:
29 CFR 1910.145 is OSHA's rule for accident prevention signs and tags in general industry. It sorts signs by how serious the hazard is, sets the colors for each type, and covers how signs must be built so the sign itself is not a hazard.

The four sign types in 1910.145

TypeWhen to use itColors
DangerOnly where an immediate hazard exists and special precautions are needed.Red, black and white.
CautionTo warn of potential hazards or caution against unsafe practices.Yellow background with a black panel and yellow letters. Any letters on the yellow background are black.
Safety instructionWhere there is a need for general instructions and suggestions about safety measures.White background with a green panel and white letters. Any letters on the white background are black.
Biological hazardTo signal the actual or potential presence of a biohazard, and to mark equipment, containers and rooms that hold infectious agents.Fluorescent orange or orange-red, with the biohazard symbol in a contrasting color.

OSHA is clear that danger signs are for real, immediate hazards. Using DANGER for a minor issue teaches people to ignore the red header, so match the header to the hazard.

How the sign itself must be made

  • Rounded or blunt corners, with no sharp edges, burrs, splinters or other sharp projections.
  • Bolt heads and other fasteners placed so they do not create a hazard.
  • Wording that is concise, easy to read and contains enough information to be understood. OSHA prefers positive statements over negative ones where it makes sense.

Can I use ANSI Z535 signs instead?

Yes. In 2013 OSHA updated 1910.145 to reference ANSI Z535.1-2006 (R2011), Z535.2-2011 and Z535.5-2011 alongside the older 1968 ANSI standards. Employers can follow either the older OSHA format or the current ANSI Z535 format, which adds WARNING (orange) and NOTICE (blue) headers and the safety alert symbol. See our ANSI Z535 page.

Tags: 1910.145 also covers accident prevention tags (DO NOT START, DANGER, CAUTION and similar) used as a temporary means of warning until a hazard is fixed. Tags are not a replacement for a permanent sign where the hazard is permanent.

page.title: ANSI Z535 Safety Sign Requirements: Signal Words, Colors and Layout
page.body:
ANSI Z535 is the American standard series for safety colors, signs, symbols, labels and tags. OSHA recognizes the Z535 format, and it is the layout most trained workers expect to see.

The parts of the Z535 series

PartCovers
Z535.1Safety colors (the exact red, orange, yellow, green, blue and others)
Z535.2Environmental and facility safety signs (the signs on walls, doors and equipment)
Z535.3Safety symbols
Z535.4Product safety signs and labels (what a manufacturer puts on a machine)
Z535.5Safety tags and barricade tapes for temporary hazards
Z535.6Safety information in manuals and instructions

Signal words

Signal wordMeaningHeader
DANGERWill result in death or serious injury if not avoided. For the most extreme hazards.Red with white letters
WARNINGCould result in death or serious injury if not avoided.Orange with black letters
CAUTIONCould result in minor or moderate injury if not avoided.Yellow with black letters
NOTICEInformation not related to personal injury, such as property damage, security or procedures. No safety alert symbol.Blue with white italic letters
SAFETY INSTRUCTIONSSafe work practices, and the location of safety equipment like first aid, eyewash and exits.Green with white letters

The safety alert symbol (a triangle with an exclamation point) goes in front of DANGER, WARNING and CAUTION when the hazard can hurt a person. It is not used with NOTICE.

What a good Z535 sign says

A Z535.2 message tells the reader three things: what the hazard is, what can happen if they ignore it, and how to avoid it. A symbol can carry part of that message, which helps workers who read another language.

Example: Arc flash and shock hazard
Can cause severe burns or death
Arc-rated PPE required beyond this point

Is Z535 required by law?

ANSI Z535 is a voluntary consensus standard. It becomes enforceable where a rule references it. OSHA 1910.145 and 1926.200 accept the 2011 editions as an option, and courts and inspectors often treat it as the expected practice. Some OSHA chemical standards (asbestos, silica, lead) set their own exact wording that must be used as written. See regulated area signs.

    WARNING header for a hazard that could kill or seriously injure.

  • CAUTIONPinch Point

    CAUTION header for a minor or moderate injury hazard.

  • NOTICERestricted Area, Authorized Access Only

    NOTICE header for a rule that is not about injury.

  • SAFETY FIRSTEyewash Station

    Safety instruction header for the location of safety equipment.

page.title: OSHA Exit Sign Requirements (1910.37): Exit, Not an Exit and Exit Route Signs
page.body:
29 CFR 1910.37 covers how exit routes are kept and marked in general industry. The sign rules are short and specific.

What 1910.37(b) requires

  • Mark every exit. Each exit must be clearly visible and marked by a sign reading "Exit."
  • Keep the line of sight open. The line of sight to an exit sign must be clearly visible at all times, and exit route doors must be free of decorations or signs that hide them.
  • Show the way. Where the direction to the nearest exit is not immediately apparent, post signs along the exit access showing the way.
  • Mark doors that are not exits. Any doorway or passage that could be mistaken for an exit must be marked "Not an Exit" or a similar designation, or be marked with its actual use, such as "Closet."
  • Light it. Each exit sign must be illuminated to at least five foot-candles (54 lux) by a reliable light source and be distinctive in color. Self-luminous or electroluminescent signs with a surface value of at least 0.06 footlamberts are allowed.
  • Size the letters. The word "Exit" must be in plainly legible letters at least six inches high, with principal strokes at least three-fourths of an inch wide.

OSHA also lets an employer comply by following NFPA 101, the Life Safety Code, instead (1910.35). Many local fire codes follow NFPA 101 or the International Fire Code, so check with your fire marshal.

What our signs cover: the lit EXIT sign over the door should be a listed illuminated or photoluminescent unit. Our aluminum signs handle the rest of the job: Not an Exit doors, keep exit clear reminders, assembly points and AED locations. OSHA has also said the ISO running-man exit symbol may be shown next to the required word "Exit."

Keep the route clear

1910.37(a) requires exit routes to be free and unobstructed, with no materials or equipment placed in them, even temporarily. A keep clear sign at doors that collect pallets and carts is one of the cheapest fixes for a common citation.

page.title: OSHA HazCom 1910.1200 Sign and Label Requirements
page.body:
The Hazard Communication Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1200, is how OSHA makes sure workers know what chemicals they work with. It is one of the most cited OSHA standards every year.

The four parts that matter for signs and labels

  • Shipped containers carry the manufacturer's GHS label: product name, signal word, hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements and supplier contact.
  • Workplace containers you fill or transfer into must be labeled with the product identifier and enough hazard information, through words, pictures and symbols, to tell workers the hazards.
  • Stationary process containers, like tanks and vats, may use signs, placards, process sheets or batch tickets instead of an affixed label, as long as they carry the same information and are readily available to workers during each shift.
  • Safety data sheets must be readily accessible to workers in their work area during each shift. A sign at the SDS binder or terminal shows where they are.

GHS pictograms

HazCom uses the GHS pictograms: a black symbol on a white background inside a red diamond border. OSHA requires eight of them. The environment pictogram is allowed but not required.

PictogramMeans
Health hazardCarcinogen, mutagen, reproductive toxicity, respiratory sensitizer, target organ toxicity, aspiration toxicity
FlameFlammables, pyrophorics, self-heating, emits flammable gas, self-reactives, organic peroxides
Exclamation markIrritant, skin sensitizer, acute toxicity (harmful), narcotic effects, respiratory tract irritant
Gas cylinderGases under pressure
CorrosionSkin corrosion and burns, eye damage, corrosive to metals
Exploding bombExplosives, self-reactives, organic peroxides
Flame over circleOxidizers
Skull and crossbonesAcute toxicity (fatal or toxic)
Do not mix up the numbers. GHS hazard categories run from 1 (most severe) down. NFPA 704 ratings run from 0 up to 4 (most severe). They are not interchangeable. See NFPA 704.

Where signs help most

Chemical storage rooms, corrosive dosing areas, flammable cabinets and the SDS station. These signs do not replace container labels, but they give a warning before someone opens the door.

page.title: NFPA 704 Diamond Requirements: Colors, Numbers, Placement and Size
page.body:
NFPA 704 is the four-color diamond firefighters look for before they go into a building. It rates the hazards of the materials inside so responders can decide how to approach a fire or spill.

The four quadrants

PositionColorRates
LeftBlueHealth hazard
TopRedFlammability
RightYellowInstability (reactivity)
BottomWhiteSpecial hazards: W with a line through it (reacts with water), OX (oxidizer), SA (simple asphyxiant gas)

Each colored quadrant gets a number from 0 (minimal hazard) to 4 (severe hazard). Ratings come from the material's properties and its SDS. Never copy the GHS category numbers from section 2 of an SDS onto the diamond. GHS runs the other way, with 1 as the worst.

When is it required?

NFPA 704 is required when another code or your local fire official requires it. Many fire codes do, including NFPA 1 and the International Fire Code for hazardous materials, and codes like NFPA 30 (flammable liquids) and NFPA 55 (compressed gases). Your fire marshal is the authority having jurisdiction.

Where to post it

NFPA 704 calls for placards in locations approved by the fire official, at a minimum:

  • On two exterior walls or enclosures that contain a way into the building or facility
  • At each access to a room or area
  • At each principal access to an outdoor storage area

How big?

Size depends on how far away it must be read. The larger the viewing distance, the bigger the numbers. A common reference is numbers about one inch tall for 50 feet, growing from there. Ask your fire official what distance they expect.

We do not make NFPA 704 placards. Pair your diamonds with clear plain-English signs at the same doors, so workers and visitors also know what is inside.

page.title: Confined Space Sign Requirements: OSHA 1910.146 and 1926.1203
page.body:
If your workplace has permit-required confined spaces, OSHA requires you to tell the people exposed to them that the spaces exist, where they are and how dangerous they are.

What the rule says

Under 29 CFR 1910.146(c)(2), the employer must inform exposed employees by posting danger signs or by any other equally effective means. OSHA gives this wording as an example that would satisfy the requirement:

Danger
Permit-required confined space
Do not enter

The construction rule, 29 CFR 1926.1203(b), has the same requirement for job sites.

What counts as permit-required

A confined space is large enough to enter, has limited ways in or out, and is not designed for continuous occupancy. It is permit-required if it also has, or could have, one of these:

  • A hazardous atmosphere (low oxygen, toxic or flammable gas)
  • Material that could engulf someone, like grain, sand or water
  • Walls that slope inward or a floor that narrows and could trap someone
  • Any other serious safety or health hazard

Common examples: tanks, silos, grain bins, pits, vaults, manholes, lift stations, sewers and boilers.

Where to post

At each entry point: the hatch, manway, door or ladder. If the space has more than one entry, sign every one. Outdoor signs should be aluminum so they survive weather and washdown.

page.title: Lockout/Tagout Sign and Tag Requirements: OSHA 1910.147
page.body:
29 CFR 1910.147, the control of hazardous energy, is how OSHA keeps machines from starting while someone is working on them. It is on OSHA's most-cited list every year.

What the rule requires

  • A written energy control program with machine-specific procedures
  • Lockout and tagout devices that are durable, standardized (by color, shape or size), substantial and identify the person who applied them
  • Tags that warn against energizing the equipment, with a legend such as Do Not Start, Do Not Open, Do Not Close, Do Not Energize, Do Not Operate
  • Training for authorized and affected employees, and periodic inspections at least once a year

Are permanent LOTO signs required?

1910.147 does not require a permanent wall sign. The lock and tag are the required devices. But permanent signs fill real gaps:

  • On machines that can start automatically or remotely, a danger sign warns anyone who reaches in.
  • At the lockout station, a sign marks where locks, tags and procedures are kept.
  • At energy isolation points (disconnects, valves), a sign reminds workers the device must be locked out, not just switched off.
Remember: a sign or tag is never a substitute for a lock where the equipment can be locked out.

page.title: Electrical Room and Panel Sign Requirements: OSHA 1910.303, NEC 110.16 and 110.26
page.body:
Electrical signs come from two places: OSHA's electrical rules for the workplace, and the National Electrical Code that your electrician and inspector follow.

OSHA 1910.303

  • Rooms with exposed live parts. Entrances to rooms and other guarded locations containing exposed live parts must be marked with conspicuous warning signs forbidding unqualified persons to enter.
  • Working space. Sufficient access and working space must be kept around electric equipment, and that space may not be used for storage.

NEC 110.26: clear space in front of panels

The NEC sets the working space in front of panels and switchgear. For most equipment up to 150 volts to ground, the clear depth is at least 3 feet (36 inches), with more required at higher voltages and some conditions. The space must stay clear. A floor marking and a keep-clear sign stop it from turning into storage.

NEC 110.16: arc flash warning

Switchboards, switchgear, panelboards, meter socket enclosures and motor control centers that are likely to be examined, adjusted, serviced or maintained while energized must be field-marked to warn qualified persons of potential arc flash hazards. NFPA 70E covers the label details and the PPE needed inside the arc flash boundary.

Substations and fenced equipment

Utility substations follow the National Electrical Safety Code, which calls for safety signs at entrances and on fences. A danger sign every few panels of fence, plus at gates, is standard practice.

page.title: Eyewash and Emergency Shower Sign Requirements: OSHA 1910.151(c) and ANSI Z358.1
page.body:
If someone can get a corrosive chemical in their eyes or on their body, they need water fast. OSHA requires the station. ANSI Z358.1 explains how to place and mark it.

OSHA 1910.151(c)

Where the eyes or body of any person may be exposed to injurious corrosive materials, suitable facilities for quick drenching or flushing of the eyes and body must be provided within the work area for immediate emergency use. Battery charging areas have their own flushing requirement under 1910.178(g).

ANSI Z358.1 in plain words

  • Close: reachable within about 10 seconds, which works out to roughly 55 feet of walking.
  • Same level as the hazard, with a clear path and no doors or obstacles in the way where possible.
  • Well lit and marked with a highly visible sign.
  • Tested weekly by activating it to flush the line and confirm it works.
  • Delivers tepid water and a 15-minute flush.

The sign matters because the person who needs the eyewash often cannot see well. Coworkers have to find it for them, fast.

page.title: Fire Extinguisher Sign Requirements: OSHA 1910.157 and NFPA 10
page.body:
Extinguishers only help if people can find them in a few seconds, through smoke, in a building they may not know.

OSHA 1910.157

  • Portable extinguishers must be mounted, located and identified so they are readily accessible without exposing employees to injury.
  • Travel distance to a Class A extinguisher may not exceed 75 feet. For Class B hazards it is 50 feet.
  • Extinguishers must get a visual inspection monthly and maintenance yearly.

NFPA 10

NFPA 10 says extinguishers must be conspicuously located and readily accessible, and kept clear of anything that blocks access or view. In large rooms, and anywhere visual obstructions cannot be avoided, a means to show the extinguisher location must be provided. A sign mounted high above the extinguisher, or a projecting sign seen down the aisle, is the usual answer.

Tips that pass inspections

  • Mount the sign high enough to be seen over racking, equipment and people.
  • Use a projecting or angled sign in long aisles so it reads from both directions.
  • Keep the floor area in front clear. A do not block sign stops pallets from landing there.

page.title: OSHA Regulated Area Sign Requirements: Silica, Asbestos and Lead Legends
page.body:
Some OSHA chemical standards do not just say "post a sign." They spell out the exact words. For these, a generic danger sign is not enough.

Respirable crystalline silica: 1910.1053

Post signs at all entrances to regulated areas, where exposure is or could be over the permissible exposure limit, bearing this legend:

Danger
Respirable crystalline silica
May cause cancer
Causes damage to lungs
Wear respiratory protection in this area
Authorized personnel only

Asbestos: 1910.1001

Warning signs go at each regulated area and at all approaches, so people can read them and take protective steps before entering:

Danger
Asbestos
May cause cancer
Causes damage to lungs
Authorized personnel only

Where respirators and protective clothing are required, the sign must also say so. Signs with the old legend ("Cancer and lung disease hazard") were only allowed until June 1, 2016.

Lead: 1910.1025

Post in each work area where exposure is above the permissible exposure limit:

Danger
Lead work area
May damage fertility or the unborn child

Do not eat, drink or smoke in this area

page.title: Construction Site Sign Requirements: OSHA 1926.200
page.body:
29 CFR 1926.200 is the construction version of OSHA's sign rule. Job sites change every day, so signs have to be visible whenever the hazard exists and come down when it is gone.

What 1926.200 covers

  • General: signs and symbols must be visible at all times when work is being performed, and removed or covered promptly when the hazard no longer exists.
  • Danger signs for immediate hazards, and caution signs for potential hazards or unsafe practices, following ANSI Z35.1-1968 or Z535.2-2011.
  • Exit signs, when required, lettered in legible red letters at least 6 inches high on a white field, with principal strokes at least 3/4 inch wide.
  • Safety instruction signs and directional signs.

  • Accident prevention tags as a temporary means of warning of an existing hazard, like defective tools or equipment.

page.title: Forklift, Aisle and Battery Charging Sign Requirements: OSHA 1910.176 and 1910.178
page.body:
Forklifts are among OSHA's most-cited standards, and warehouses get hurt where people and lift trucks share the same space.

Battery charging areas: 1910.178(g)

  • Charging must be done in areas designated for that purpose.
  • Facilities must be provided for flushing and neutralizing spilled electrolyte, for fire protection, for protecting chargers from damage by trucks, and for adequate ventilation to disperse fumes from gassing batteries.
  • Smoking is prohibited in the charging area, and precautions must be taken to prevent open flames, sparks or electric arcs there.

Operators: 1910.178(l)

Only trained and evaluated operators may drive powered industrial trucks. A sign at the truck parking area and at the keys sets the rule where it counts.

Aisles and storage: 1910.176

  • Where mechanical handling equipment is used, aisles and passageways must have sufficient safe clearance and be kept clear. Permanent aisles must be appropriately marked.
  • Storage must be stable and secure against sliding or collapse.
  • Clearance signs must be provided to warn of clearance limits.
